urban-data-s1.title: Census figures for the East Ridge neighborhood

table.caption: East Ridge census tract, an invented neighborhood (invented data for practice)
rows: Share of homes rented, not owned
Share of residents who moved in during the last 5 years

urban-data-s2.title: Interviews with East Ridge residents
urban-data-s2.text:
Invented interviews for practice, 2026.

Rosa, 68, renter for 40 years: "My rent went up three times in four years. Most of my friends from church have moved to the suburbs. I still love this street, but it does not feel like mine."

Marcus, 34, bought a house in 2019: "We picked East Ridge for the old houses and the bus line downtown. The neighbors were kind to us, but I know some people see us as the reason prices went up."

Mr. Tran, owner of a corner store since 1995: "Sales are up, but my old customers are gone. The new ones want different things."

items.q: Which trend from 2000 to 2020 does the table show?
options: Population more than doubled
The share of renters rose
Rent and income both rose sharply
Fewer residents were newcomers

why.correct: Median rent rose from 650 to 1,450 dollars and median income from 31,000 to 72,000 dollars, while population barely changed.
options: Population changed little, from 4,200 to 4,300.
The share of renters fell, from 78% to 58%.
Right: both more than doubled.
The share of newcomers rose, from 20% to 46%.

items.q: Between 2010 and 2020, which measure changed the most in percent terms?
options: Population, up about 8%
Median household income, up about 90%
Share of homes rented, down about 50%
Median rent, up about 20%

why.correct: Income rose from 38,000 to 72,000 dollars: about 89%, close to 90%. Rent rose about 81%, population about 8%.
options: Population rose about 8%, much less than income.
The renting share fell 16 points, from 74% to 58%, not by half.
Rent rose from 800 to 1,450 dollars, about 81%.

items.q: Which question can the census table NOT answer?
options: Why long-time residents moved away
How much median rent rose
Whether the share of renters fell
How many people lived there in 2010

why.correct: The table counts people and homes but records no reasons or feelings. Interviews are needed for why.
options: Right: reasons for moving are not in a census table.
The table gives rent for each year.
The table gives the renting share for each year.
The table gives 4,000 for 2010.

items.q: At what scale are the data in the table?
options: National: the whole country
Global: many countries
Regional: a group of states
Local: one census tract

why.correct: The data describe one census tract, a neighborhood of a few thousand people: the local scale.
options: A whole country would have millions of people, not 4,300.
Only one neighborhood is shown.
A tract is far smaller than a group of states.
Right: one small area inside a city.

items.q: What kind of data do the interviews provide?
options: Quantitative census counts
Survey estimates with margins of error
Qualitative data on attitudes
Remote sensing images

why.correct: Interviews give words, feelings and reasons from a few people: qualitative data.
options: Census counts are numbers for everyone in an area.
Surveys ask a fixed set of questions of a sample and report numbers.
Right: personal accounts of how change feels.
The interviews are spoken accounts, not satellite images.

items.q: What do the interviews show that the census table does not?
options: That median rent rose
How residents feel about the change
That the share of renters fell
How many people live in East Ridge

why.correct: The table shows rising rent and income; only the interviews show loss of community, a newcomer's view and a shop owner's mixed feelings.
options: The table already shows rising rent.
Right: meaning and attitudes come from qualitative data.
The table already shows the renting share fell.
The table gives the population.

items.q: What is the main limit of using these three interviews to describe the whole neighborhood?
options: Three people may not represent its 4,300
Interviews give too many numbers
People tend to be less honest in interviews
The people interviewed live outside East Ridge

why.correct: A small sample of interviews can reveal views and reasons, but it cannot show how common those views are across thousands of residents.
options: Right: a small sample cannot stand for everyone.
Interviews give words, not many numbers.
Honesty is not the issue here; the limit is how few people were asked.
All three people live or work in East Ridge.

items.q: Mr. Tran says "sales are up, but my old customers are gone." How does this fit the census table?
options: It contradicts the table, which shows incomes falling
It shows the population fell sharply
It shows rents fell as stores did better
Higher incomes and many newcomers explain both

why.correct: Incomes more than doubled and 46% of residents were newcomers by 2020: richer new customers raise sales while older customers leave.
options: The table shows incomes rising, not falling.
The population rose slightly.
The table shows rents rising.
Right: the numbers and the story agree.

items.q: Which is an example of survey data?
options: A geographer's notes from walking a street
A resident's life story
Answers from a sample of households to set questions
A satellite image of a city at night

why.correct: Survey data come from asking a sample of people the same set of questions, such as the American Community Survey.
options: Field notes are qualitative observation.
A life story is a narrative, qualitative data.
Right: a sample and fixed questions make a survey.
A satellite image is remote sensing.

items.q: The American Community Survey reports that median rent in one small tract rose by 2% from one year to the next, with a margin of error of plus or minus 6%. What can you conclude?
options: Rent rose by exactly 2%
The data cannot show whether rent really changed
Rent fell by 6%
The survey counted each household

why.correct: The change (2%) is smaller than the margin of error (6%), so the true change could be up, down or none. Survey estimates for small areas need care.
options: The 2% is an estimate, not an exact figure.
Right: the change is inside the margin of error.
Nothing shows a 6% fall; 6% is the margin of error.
The ACS asks a sample, not every household.

items.q: A city's average rent rose 5% over ten years, but rent in one census tract doubled. Why does the citywide figure hide the change?
options: Citywide data average many tracts together
The tract was counted twice
Citywide data come from interviews
The tract is outside the city

why.correct: Aggregated data combine many neighborhoods into one number, so a sharp change in one tract is diluted. Name the scale of the data.
options: Right: aggregation hides local differences.
Nothing suggests a double count.
Citywide averages come from census or survey numbers.
The tract is one of the city's own.

items.q: A researcher wants to learn why families left a neighborhood after their landlord sold the building. Which method fits best?
options: A census count of the neighborhood
A satellite image of the block
A map of median income by tract
Interviews with families who left

why.correct: The question asks why, so it needs reasons in people's own words: interviews.
options: A census count shows how many left, not why.
An image shows buildings, not reasons.
An income map shows patterns, not reasons.
Right: reasons come from qualitative data.

items.q: A planner wants to know which of the city's 200 census tracts had the fastest rise in rent from 2010 to 2020. Which source fits best?
options: Interviews with ten residents
One resident's mental map
Census and survey data by tract
A walk through one neighborhood

why.correct: Comparing 200 tracts on one measure over time needs consistent numbers for each tract: census and survey data.
options: Ten interviews cannot cover 200 tracts.
A mental map shows one person's view.
Right: numbers by tract allow fair comparison.
One walk covers one neighborhood.

items.q: Which of these are qualitative data about a neighborhood? Select all that apply.
options: An oral history from a long-time resident
Field notes on which shops have closed
Median household income for the tract
The share of homes that are rented

why.correct: Qualitative data are words, stories and observations; incomes and shares are quantitative.
options: Right: an oral history is a narrative.
Right: field notes are observation in words.
Income is a number from a census or survey.
A share is a number from a census or survey.

items.q: Build a statement comparing what census data and interviews show about a changing neighborhood.

specific.frame: Census data show ___, whereas interviews show ___.
specific.model: Census data show that median rent in the East Ridge tract more than doubled from 2000 to 2020, whereas interviews show that long-time renters like Rosa feel the street no longer belongs to them.

sideA.label: What census data show
options: that median rent in the East Ridge tract more than doubled from 2000 to 2020
why each family chose to move away

why.1: A census records counts, not each family's reasons.

sideB.label: What interviews show
options: that long-time renters like Rosa feel the street no longer belongs to them
the exact median income of the whole tract

why.1: An exact median income for the tract comes from census or survey numbers.

why.correct: A compare speaks of both sources and says how they differ.
